Eyes for the Blind

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight on Carte Blanche: Sight is something we all take for granted. But have you ever stopped to think what it must be like to live a world of darkness? John Webb has the story.

Unique Selling Point:
Our story will be told through the eyes of the visually impaired, their fears, their hopes and their challenges. What role does society play in aggravating their circumstances further and why are we allowing blatant discrimination against the visually impaired to continue? We will ask the questions to those who transgress and ask for comment from the wrongdoers

Summary:
To the visually impaired every day is a challenge. Meet Theo. He lives in Paarl and works at the Maternity Hospital in Salt River. At 6h00 every morning Theo and his guide dog Chad, takes the train from Paarl station to Cape Town central during which he encounters many obstacles. He relies on Chad to guide him through the hordes of people to the correct platform and often the trains are switched or late, says Theo.
Taxi’s and busses are the worst, he says. I have been told by Golden Arrow bus driver to purchase a ticket for Chad as he is passenger too. Most of the taxi drivers don’t allow my dog as they have an inherent distrust in dogs and some the passengers are scared of dogs. It does not matter how many times I have to tell them that he is a gentle dog and will not bite.
Transport is a major problem for the visually impaired as Andre Neethling has told us. Andre and his trusted friend Emmie relies on taxis and often catches an Uber to work, as he is not on the main taxi line. On several occasions Uber drivers have left him standing in the rain and in the cold. They refuse to pick me up and still insist on charging a cancellation fee. The closest I get to lodge my complaint with Uber is via email, as they have never bothered picking up the phone to apologise personally. The best they are prepared to do is to apologise on email for the inconvenience and refund my money.
Meet Michelle Botha. She holds a master’s degree in Gender Studies from UCT and works for the Institute of the Blind in Cape Town. Michelle’s positive attitude is inspiring and she does not let the hindrances of being blind disable her. But there have been times she says, where I have felt so despondent when people’s insensitive nature and ignorance has caused me great pain. Time and time again restaurant managers turn friends and I away because of my guide dog. It is so infuriating! I am a paying customer too. Is my money not worth it, she exclaims.



Further information:
Discrimination in the daily life of the visually impaired starts from the moment they leave home. At the bank or in the shopping mall or at the grocery store around the corner, the man in the security uniform refuse the dog entrance and so the owner has to ‘ask to speak to the manager’ to gain access. Instructed by the company’s ‘no dog allowed’ policy security guards do not receive the necessary training to differentiate between normal and working dogs. They simply follow the rules in fear of being fired by the owner. It is the responsibility of the security company to ensure that they have been trained properly.
Sitting down for a meal at a restaurant or simply having a cup of coffee becomes a nightmare, says Michelle. There are only a few franchise restaurants that extend a hand of welcome. Wimpy and Spur have a brail menu so I know that will be a safe bet but if I want to upscale to a more sophisticated venue ninety percent of the time the answer will simply be NO. Sometimes I fight for my right as a citizen to have access to the places a normal person but I have come to realise that the indented discrimination against the visually impaired with their dogs will remain an issue in my life. So you try and deal with it, explains Michelle.

Press Release:


Would you manage to navigate the chaos that is public life without our sense of sight? From crossing busy intersections, getting through noise shopping centers, train, taxi an bus stations and more, blind South Africans daily face this reality. Often, their only means of independence is a highly trained service animal and trusted companion, their guide dog. Carte Blanche spends time with the visually impaired to experience a society often insensitive and unreasonable to the blind and their guides.

Script:


Insert: Eyes for the blind


V/O: Theo Louis has been blind for most of his life, after a freak soccer accident as a teenager left him with severed optic nerves. He lives in Paarl, about 60 km outside Cape Town. Each day Theo and his guide dog, Chad, catch four trains to and from work.

Up audio John: Let’s just hold up here. Let’s just pause.

V/O Crossing at this particular intersection is perilous because the traffic light isn’t fitted with an audio signal.

John: So ordinarily Theo you would need someone to help you across?

Theo: Yes it is impossible for me alone to get over here.

V/O We joined Theo on his afternoon walk to the Mowbray train station, from where he makes the short trip to Cape Town for his late afternoon connection to Paarl.

Up audio: Train pulling into station.

V/O Once on the train, Theo still has to negotiate his way to an empty seat –a task that often irritates his fellow passengers.

John: Do they get angry with you.

Theo: Yes they do but they don’t try and help me to find a seat.

V/O While improvements have been made in accommodating people with disabilities, using public transport often isn’t as uneventful as the first part of Theo’s journey has been. Andre Neethling lost his sight at a young age due to Macular Degeneration.

Andre up audio: Ok Emmie, let’s go. Straight on find the curb.

Link: The visually impaired have to rely heavily on the public transport system and for Andre that means having to catch taxis, but that can be a long and frustrating process.

V/O Andre is fiercely independent and has fine tuned his hearing skills to differentiate sounds.

Andre up audio: It’s one of those taxis. Toots he is available but won’t stop.

Andre up audio: They just locked the door!

V/O Eventually Andre gets lucky.

Up Audio Andre: You don’t need to be scared. It’s a guide dog.

V/O Andre finds that many taxi drivers are nervous about his dog, not realising it is a specially trained service animal. Alarmingly, it’s not a misunderstanding limited to the minibus taxi industry, as we discovered when Ross Crymble took a MyCity bus from Melkbos into Cape Town. It’s a journey he would once easily have made on his own, were it not for a life-shattering motorbike accident 8 years ago. Ross now heavily relies on the assistance of his guide dog Ferdi.

John: I guess you have a special relationship with your dog.

Ross Crymble: You can say it is like my kid, and he is my eyes and wherever I goes he goes.

V/O And so it was that Ross took the bus into Cape Town.

Ross: No dogs allowed but I am blind people are allowed to have dogs.

Bus driver: This dog is not allowed on the bus.

Ross: Then how come it says on your MyCity website “guide dogs allowed”. You can see his collar here, he is a guide dog.

Bus driver: No he is not allowed.

V/O Ross’s friend Sarah Gee often accompanies him on these trips. She says this incident isn’t uncommon.

Sarah Gee: So for the last 3 weeks that we have been trying to catch a bus with a guide dog there have been incidences every week. Last week the driver point blank refused to allow us on the bus and Ross literally had to take his glasses off and said: “I can’t see, this dog is my eyes, it is a guide dog it is not a pet it is a working dog.”

Bus driver up audio: Who does this dog belong to?

Ross: It belongs to me it is my guide dog.

Bus driver: But it is not allowed to the bus here.

Ross: From the word go it had made me not want to do it. Like the confrontations I had with the drivers, by the time I get home I am so flustered, fed-up you know.

V/O Worryingly Ross had a similar but more frightening experience with a MyCity bus driver about a year ago.

Ross Crymble: The bus came, the door opened up, and as I was climbing on with Ferdi my guide dog, the driver was like ‘ah no dogs, no dogs” and just closed the door on Ferdi’s head basically and I was scooted off the bus.

John: So he pushed you off?

Ross: Yeh. Very aggressive.Yeh even the people on the bus, we’ve got to go.

V/O Brett Herron is Cape Town’s Mayoral Committee member for Transport. While his department does not have direct oversight of MyCity’s drivers, he was appalled by Ross’s story.

Brett Herron: Well it is shocking learning to me. We have designed this entire system to be universally accessible. Our policies are clear. So if I had been aware of any incident where a guide dog or a visually impaired person with a guide dog was refused access because of the dog then we could have taken corrective steps with the vehicle operating company either through the penalty system or through training.

V/O The City has since told us all busses have been fitted with stickers specifying the guide dogs are allowed on board. The bus operators who oversee the drivers have also been reminded of the policy. It remains to be seen whether these steps have an impact on behaviour which Pieter van Niekerk, from The SA Guide Dog’s
Association, describes as ‘not uncommon’.

Pieter van Niekerk: It is definitely not isolated. We constantly get reports from guide dog owners where they have been denied access but part of our training with the guide dog owners also is to take action whenever they get stopped or denied access.

V/O But, that kind of confrontation is something Michelle Botha would prefer to avoid. A Retinitis Pigmentosa sufferer, she initially used a cane to help navigate everyday obstacles but now, thanks to her guide dog, Panda, her horizons have been widened.

Michelle: The most important thing she has given me is freedom of movement without having to rely on someone else.

V/O But having a guide dog presents its own difficulties.

Michelle: Often I encounter a negativity towards my dog and I think it is hugely around education.

V/O Ignorance towards the needs of a blind person could have contributed to the way in which Michelle was treated when we accompanied her on a recent shopping trip where she visited the Vodacom store. Notice how she is simply ignored.

Michelle Botha: In that situation Panda had walked me to the door but once in the store I felt as if I was invisible.

V/O It took our producer to point out that Michelle needed help.

Up audio Vodacom Assistant: Can I help you?

Up audio: Michelle Botha: Yes please. I just want some information.

John Webb: So they gave you a little slip with the number and if your number is called you will say here I am and then you will be served.

Michelle Botha: Or that is when you need to go to the counter and I don’t know where that counter is.

John: I suppose training and education is one thing but much should be guided around common sense.

Michelle: Absolutely and I find where I really had wonderful experiences in terms of customer service has been with individuals who use a bit of common sense around “if I were in that person’s shoes, if I would not see, what would I need in order to access this service.”

V/O In a written response Vodacom apologised and explained that their system is designed to accommodate the disabled. But it’s unlikely this will be the last humiliation suffered by Michelle, particularly when you consider that, just days later, Andre encountered similar ignorance while trying to buy groceries.

Trident Security guard: But that dog is not allowed to come in.

Andre Neethling: Why is this dog not allowed to come in? I am blind, it is a guide dog.

V/O Thankfully, a Woolworths’ staff member came to Andre’s aid.

Pieter van Niekerk: That in my personal opinion is where the majority of these problems lie where we deal with security staff they are uninformed, they apply the rule of no dogs allowed.

V/O In response, Woolworths said the visually impaired and their guide dogs were welcome in their stores. Trident Security says it is investigating the matter.

Up audio intercom gong sounding.

V/O Back in Cape Town, Theo and Chad negotiate the busy concourse to catch their afternoon train to Paarl.

LINK: So today I was Theo’s guide as he made his way here to platform ten but
ordinarily he has to rely on the help of strangers to tell him which platform to go to which can very often change at the last minute.

V/O And as we leave Theo and Chad it’s clear society still has a long way to go in changing attitudes towards the blind.

Pieter: It is definitely a fact where we often get excluded or limitation gets put on us and in think society should actually take the lead there and say how can we change that, how can we make our customers and our staff and our security aware about the wonderful work done by a guide dog.

END

The best they are prepared to do is to apologise on email for the inconvenience and refund my money. Meet Michelle Botha. She holds a master’s degree in Gender Studies from UCT and works for the Institute of the Blind in Cape Town. Michelle’s positive attitude is inspiring and she does not let the hindrances of being blind disable her. But there have been times she says, where I have felt so despondent when people’s insensitive nature and ignorance has caused me great pain. Time and time again restaurant managers turn friends and I away because of my guide dog. It is so infuriating! I am a paying customer too. Is my money not worth it, she exclaims.
metadata.Further information: Discrimination in the daily life of the visually impaired starts from the moment they leave home. At the bank or in the shopping mall or at the grocery store around the corner, the man in the security uniform refuse the dog entrance and so the owner has to ‘ask to speak to the manager’ to gain access. Instructed by the company’s ‘no dog allowed’ policy security guards do not receive the necessary training to differentiate between normal and working dogs. They simply follow the rules in fear of being fired by the owner. It is the responsibility of the security company to ensure that they have been trained properly. Sitting down for a meal at a restaurant or simply having a cup of coffee becomes a nightmare, says Michelle. There are only a few franchise restaurants that extend a hand of welcome. Wimpy and Spur have a brail menu so I know that will be a safe bet but if I want to upscale to a more sophisticated venue ninety percent of the time the answer will simply be NO. Sometimes I fight for my right as a citizen to have access to the places a normal person but I have come to realise that the indented discrimination against the visually impaired with their dogs will remain an issue in my life. So you try and deal with it, explains Michelle.
